transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-18
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 53m
Attendees: Samira Kahn (Redwood AE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Ravi Patel (CTO - CopperBay), Elena Morris (Platform Eng), Tomas Yu (SRE Lead)

Brief summary:
CopperBay is evaluating Redwood for a mixed workload: low-latency chat (p95 target 120-200ms), plus bursty batch scoring for analytics pipelines (token/sec spikes). They want guidance on Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC), expected p95 and tokens/sec for their model family, and network/SSO/security constraints for a Q4 pilot. SE asked for traces and sample prompts; Redwood to provide pricing scenarios and a benchmark kit.

Topics discussed:
- Current stack and traffic patterns
- p95 targets and acceptable tail latency for chat vs batch
- Streaming vs non-streaming responses, token/sec baselines
- Dedicated GPU pools, autoscaling and burst options
- Private/VPC requirements, SAML, KMS, audit logs
- Fallback model variants and routing policy
- Next steps and tangible artifacts

Transcript body:
[00:00] Samira (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Samira from Redwood, and with me is Luis, our performance SE. Can you do a quick round of intros?
[00:10] Ravi (CopperBay): Yeah hi I'm Ravi, CTO, I own infra and model decisions for the product team. Elena and Tomas are my infra folks.
[00:16] Elena (CopperBay): Hi, Elena, Platform.
[00:18] Tomas (CopperBay): Tomas, SRE.
[00:20] Luis (Redwood): Nice to meet you all. Quick agenda — understand your p95 goals, traffic shape, and whether you'll need hosted or private. Then we can map to Dedicated configs and a baseline token/sec test.
[00:34] Ravi: Right — our primary concern is chat latency. We need p95 in the 120-200ms range for short replies (avg 40-80 tokens). For longer assistants it's ok to go up to 500ms, but chat is the priority. We also run daily analytics jobs that can spike 10-15x for short windows, token scoring runs.
[00:52] Samira: Got it. Does the 120-200ms p95 include network RTT? And are those numbers for end-to-end vs just inference compute?
[01:02] Ravi: That's end-to-end from our app server to response show. Our internal network is pretty fast, regionally in GCP us-west2. We assume ~30-40ms RTT normally. So inference compute should be in the 80-160ms p95 window ideally.
[01:18] Luis: Okay. A couple of clarifying Qs — what model family are you using? Large LLaMA variants, MPT, or something else? And are you using streaming token-by-token or full-response?
[01:30] Elena: We're currently on a fine-tuned LLaMA-ish model, roughly 13B in size, quantized to int8 locally. We have streaming enabled for chat, and batch non-streaming for scoring. Average seq len is 80 tokens for chat, some prompts go to 200 tokens.
[01:45] Luis: 13B with int8 — good to know. For streaming chat with avg 80 tokens we can usually hit pretty strong p95s on modern GPU infra. A few things that affect p95: batching strategy, KV cache warmness, sequence length variance, and whether you have prefix caching enabled.
[02:00] Tomas: Can you unpack prefix caching? We heard about KV cache but not sure how it maps to our workloads.
[02:05] Luis: Sure. Prefix or KV caching stores key/value states for repeated prefixes so subsequent calls bypass recomputation. For chat with repeated system instructions or standard prompts, that can drop average per-request work and help the tail. Works best when you have steady session affinity or a sticky routing.
[02:20] Ravi: Interesting. We do have lots of repeated prompts — system messages and small templates. Would Redwood's hosted API provide prefix caching or is that a Dedicated feature?
[02:30] Samira: Both. Hosted has caching heuristics but Dedicated and Private give you more control — ability to pin session affinity, customize cache TTLs, and tune the serving runtime. For strict p95 guarantees we usually recommend Dedicated pools with burst capacity.
[02:45] Elena: On Dedicated — what's the rough tokens/sec and concurrent request capacity per GPU for our model? We need numbers to size capacity.
[02:52] Luis: Ballpark for a 13B int8 model on an A100-ish class GPU: steady streaming throughput could be 300-700 tokens/sec depending on kernel & sequence mix. Concurrency depends on batch policy — with small latency SLOs we keep small micro-batches, so maybe 8-16 concurrent streams per GPU for p95 under 200ms. For non-streaming batch scoring you can get much higher token/sec if you accept higher tail latency.
[03:20] Ravi: So if we hit spikes 10x — how does Redwood handle bursts? Autoscale? Pre-warmed burst capacity?
[03:27] Samira: We have a couple of options: Dedicated reserved pools with configured burst capacity (pre-provisioned GPUs that spin up for spikes), and a burst buffer for hosted where requests route to compatible model variants — slightly cheaper/faster fallbacks. For firm SLAs on p95, reserved Dedicated with burst nodes and canary routing is the conservative approach.
[03:46] Tomas: What's the cold-start time for nodes in Dedicated? If we scale up by 10 GPUs, how long to serve?
[03:52] Luis: Cold start depends — container init and model load can be 30s to 3m depending on model size and whether quantized artifacts and checkpoint warm caches exist. We support pre-warming and keeping a minimal warm pool to avoid long cold starts.
[04:06] Elena: From security side — we require SAML SSO, KMS key control, and audit logs for any private data. Does Redwood's Private deployment support HSM-backed KMS and SOC2 attestation?
[04:18] Samira: Yes, our Private and Dedicated enterprise offering supports customer-managed KMS, integrate with HSMs in many cases, and we provide SOC 2 Type II reports. Audit logs and per-token logging controls are configurable. We'll send the security pack in the follow-up.
[04:33] Ravi: Great. Another concern: we have multi-region traffic. Can Redwood route by region? We want p95 in eu-west and us-west with failover.
[04:42] Luis: Smart routing can route by policy — latency, cost, region. For cross-region failover we recommend consistent model versions across regions and warm replicas. There is slight variance in p95 due to network, but the runtime supports automatic fallback to a compatible variant in another region.
[04:58] Samira: Quick note — do you have any compliance or data residency requirements that would force Private?
[05:03] Ravi: Not strictly yet, but enterprise customers sometimes request data residency in EU; we'd like the option for Private in eu-west for those customers later in Q4.
[05:12] Luis: Okay we'll include regions and private deploy notes.
[05:16] Tomas: Let's talk benchmarks — what's in the benchmark kit and how intrusive is it? We can't open prod.
[05:22] Luis: The kit is a small load generator, sample scripts, and a dashboard to collect p95, throughput, and token/sec. It can run against a sandbox model; we also have a mode that runs against a customer-hosted container if you want on-prem. We'll ask for a small sample of your prompts to run realistic mixes.
[05:36] Elena: We'll provide prompt sets but want to ensure we don't leak PII. Is there an option to scrub or synthetic-ize prompts?
[05:43] Samira: Absolutely — you can redact or synthesize tokens. We also accept metrics-only traces if you prefer.
[05:48] Ravi: For cost — what's the delta between Hosted and Dedicated for steady state vs spikes?
[05:54] Samira: Short answer: Hosted is great for low lift and variable traffic. Dedicated is more economical at scale and gives p95 predictability. We'll provide sample numbers in a cost worksheet — factors include reserved capacity, burst pool hours, and per-token compute for streaming.
[06:10] Luis: Also quantization profile matters; int8 vs 4-bit can change token/sec and memory footprint significantly. We can analyze tradeoffs once we see your accuracy constraints.
[06:20] Ravi: Accuracy — we can't regress quality. We need to tie any quantization to an eval suite. Do you support A/B rollouts and automatic fallback if quality drops?
[06:28] Luis: Yes, Redwood has rollout controls and canarying, with eval hooks to trigger rollback. We can also route a small percentage to a higher-precision variant.
[06:36] Elena: Networking specifics for Private: we need VPC peering and strict egress rules. How does the control plane access the private region?
[06:44] Samira: Private has an optional control plane bridge that uses customer-managed endpoints and can operate over peered networks. For air-gapped installs we ship an on-prem bundle, but that takes extra lead time.
[06:56] Tomas: Lead time — how long to set up Private vs Dedicated?
[07:00] Luis: Dedicated can be provisioned in weeks; Private on-prem or air-gapped is typically 6-12 weeks depending on networking, security reviews, and installation windows.
[07:12] Ravi: Ok that fits our Q4 pilot timeline.
[07:15] Samira: For the pilot, we typically recommend a 4-week smoke test: week 1 basic integration, week 2 run baselines, week 3 pilot load tests & SLO tuning, week 4 ramp & sign-off. Does that sound reasonable?
[07:28] Elena: Yes. We want specific p95 goals: 150ms end-to-end for chat. If you can get compute p95 under 120ms we're golden.
[07:37] Luis: We'll aim for compute p95 under 100-120ms if possible. If not, we can discuss model variant (¬smaller context/prefix caching) or Dedicated tuning.
[07:45] Ravi: One last technical Q: KV cache warmness for many small sessions — will cache help or will it be a miss-heavy workload?
[07:53] Luis: If user sessions are ephemeral it can be miss-heavy. But even per-tenant caching and partial-key caching helps in templated flows. We'll look at your session distribution.
[08:02] Samira: I'm going to call out the follow-ups: we'll send security docs, a benchmarking kit, pricing scenarios, and schedule the deep-dive. Anything else?
[08:10] Ravi: Could you also include an example SLA for p95 and an explanation of how fallback routing looks in practice?
[08:16] Samira: Yep. We'll include sample SLA language and a short diagram.
[08:20] Tomas: For the benchmark — can you simulate token bursts that emulate our batch scoring? Like 15x for 10 minutes?
[08:28] Luis: Yes we'll craft a script that runs burst windows and steady-state windows and capture p95 and packetized token/sec.
[08:34] Elena: During the meeting I noticed some micro-stutters on my side — apologies if some words were missed. We'll rely on the notes.
[08:40] Speaker 1: (inaudible)
[08:43] [09:00] Luis: Quick aside — for the streaming buffer, how are you doing partial flushes? Do you stream token-by-token or in small batches?
[09:10] Elena: Currently token-by-token with a small flush every 50ms. We can tweak.
[09:14] Luis: Small change — flushing in 2-3 token micro-batches can reduce overhead while keeping perceived latency low. We'll recommend an experiment.
[09:25] Ravi: Do you expose token-level cost on the console? We want to see per-route and per-model token costs.
[09:32] Samira: Yes, Redwood Console has token-level cost breakdowns by route/model/time and tracing. That helps attribute cost to features and tune batching.
[09:40] Tomas: What about encryption in transit between our app in GCP and Redwood Hosted? TLS only or mutual TLS?
[09:45] Luis: We support mTLS for stricter setups, plus VPN/peering for Private.
[09:49] Elena: Great. Any gotchas for model geography? If we replicate to eu-west, will model variant mismatch cause fallback errors?
[09:55] Luis: We do model version pinning and compatibility checks — automatic fallback only to compatible variants. We'll surface warnings if a variant mismatch exists.
[10:05] Ravi: Okay let's close with next week actions.
[10:10] Samira: Recap — Samira to send pricing and security docs, Luis to share benchmark kit, customer to send traces and prompts. We'll follow up with calendar invites for the SE deep-dive.
[10:20] Elena: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[10:24] Tomas: Thanks.
[10:26] Luis: Thanks, bye.

Meeting end.
